content:
# Capstone Project - Part 2: Evaluate, Deploy, Polish

##### The README that got the interview

Two students from the same cohort in Pune applied to the same startup. Both had built RAG assistants. Both had working code on GitHub.

The first repo's README said:

> # RAG Chatbot
> A chatbot using LangChain and OpenAI.
> ## Setup
> `pip install -r requirements.txt`

The second opened with:

> # ScholarshipBot — Answers Maharashtra post-matric scholarship questions in English, Hindi, and Marathi
>
> **[Live demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/...)** · **[3-min video](https://...)**
>
> 340 students used this in its first month. It answers eligibility, document,
> and deadline questions from the official 62-page PDF, citing the exact clause
> and page. Answers 20 benchmark questions at 89% accuracy with correct citations;
> refuses cleanly on all 5 out-of-scope probes; p95 latency 4.2s.
>
> ![screenshot](docs/demo.png)

The hiring manager later said he read the first line of repo one, closed it, and spent eleven minutes on repo two — including watching the video.

**Same skill level. Same techniques. Wildly different outcomes.** Part 2 is about the work that makes the difference: measuring, securing, deploying, and presenting.

##### Evaluation

You built the evaluation set on Day 43 before optimising. Now run it properly and report numbers.

```python
# eval/run_eval.py
import json, time, argparse
import pandas as pd
from ragas import evaluate
from ragas.metrics import faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision, context_recall
from datasets import Dataset

from app.rag import RAGPipeline
from app.guardrails import run_rule_checks


def load_testset(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return [json.loads(line) for line in f]


def run(testset_path, db_path):
    rag = RAGPipeline(db_path=db_path)
    tests = load_testset(testset_path)

    rows, ragas_data = [], {"question": [], "answer": [],
                            "contexts": [], "ground_truth": []}

    for tc in tests:
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        result = rag.answer(tc["question"])
        latency = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000

        contexts = [c["text"] for c in result["chunks"]]
        retrieved_pages = {c["metadata"]["page"] for c in result["chunks"]}
        expected_pages = set(tc.get("expected_pages", []))

        checks = run_rule_checks(result["answer"], "\n".join(contexts))

        rows.append({
            "id": tc["id"],
            "language": tc.get("language", "en"),
            "category": tc["category"],
            "page_hit": bool(retrieved_pages & expected_pages) if expected_pages else None,
            "has_citation": next(c.passed for c in checks if c.check == "has_citation"),
            "numbers_grounded": next(c.passed for c in checks if c.check == "numbers_grounded"),
            "refused": "not covered in the official guidelines" in result["answer"].lower(),
            "should_refuse": tc.get("should_refuse", False),
            "latency_ms": round(latency, 1),
        })

        ragas_data["question"].append(tc["question"])
        ragas_data["answer"].append(result["answer"])
        ragas_data["contexts"].append(contexts)
        ragas_data["ground_truth"].append(tc.get("ground_truth", ""))

    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df["refusal_correct"] = df["refused"] == df["should_refuse"]

    scores = evaluate(Dataset.from_dict(ragas_data),
                      metrics=[faithfulness, answer_relevancy,
                               context_precision, context_recall])

    print("\n=== Rule checks ===")
    print(f"page hit rate      {df['page_hit'].mean():.1%}")
    print(f"citation present   {df['has_citation'].mean():.1%}")
    print(f"numbers grounded   {df['numbers_grounded'].mean():.1%}")
    print(f"refusal correct    {df['refusal_correct'].mean():.1%}")
    print(f"p50 / p95 latency  {df['latency_ms'].median():.0f} / "
          f"{df['latency_ms'].quantile(0.95):.0f} ms")
    print("\n=== By language ===")
    print(df.groupby("language")[["page_hit", "has_citation"]].mean().round(3))
    print("\n=== RAGAS ===")
    print(scores)

    df.to_csv("eval/results.csv", index=False)
    return df, scores
```

**Report the breakdown, not just the headline.** "89% overall" hides that Marathi is at 71% while English is at 96% — and that gap is the single most useful finding in the whole evaluation, because it tells you exactly what to fix next.

**Include the progression table in your README.** This is the artefact that demonstrates engineering rather than luck:

| Configuration | page hit@5 | faithfulness | p95 latency |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vector only, 400-char chunks | 0.55 | 0.81 | 2.9s |
| + 800-char chunks with overlap | 0.68 | 0.84 | 3.0s |
| + heading prefixes | 0.74 | 0.87 | 3.0s |
| + hybrid search | 0.84 | 0.88 | 3.4s |
| **+ reranker** | **0.89** | **0.92** | **4.2s** |

##### Guardrails

Wire Day 40's defences into the request path — all of them, in the right order.

```python
# app/guardrails.py
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class GuardResult:
    allowed: bool
    stage: str = ""
    reason: str = ""
    message: str = ""


SAFE_REFUSAL = ("I can only answer questions about the scholarship scheme "
                "from the official guidelines.")


def guard_request(question: str) -> GuardResult:
    if len(question) > 1000:
        return GuardResult(False, "length", "too long",
                           "Please ask a shorter question.")

    if detect_injection(question)["suspicious"]:
        return GuardResult(False, "injection", "pattern match", SAFE_REFUSAL)

    mod = moderate(question)
    if mod["flagged"]:
        return GuardResult(False, "input_moderation",
                           ",".join(mod["categories"]), SAFE_REFUSAL)

    return GuardResult(True)


def guard_response(answer: str, context: str) -> GuardResult:
    checks = run_rule_checks(answer, context)
    critical = {"numbers_grounded", "no_pan", "no_aadhaar"}
    failed = [c.check for c in checks if not c.passed]

    if set(failed) & critical:
        return GuardResult(False, "grounding", ",".join(failed),
                           "I could not verify that answer against the "
                           "guidelines. Please contact your scholarship cell.")

    mod = moderate(answer)
    if mod["flagged"]:
        return GuardResult(False, "output_moderation",
                           ",".join(mod["categories"]), SAFE_REFUSAL)

    return GuardResult(True)
```

**Cheap checks first.** Length and regex run in microseconds; moderation is an API call. Ordering them this way is both faster and cheaper at scale.

**Report your false-positive rate alongside your block rate.** A system that blocks everything scores perfectly on safety and is useless. Run twenty legitimate queries through the guards and confirm none are blocked — that number belongs in your README.

##### Deployment

Day 41's Dockerfile and checklist, applied. Three capstone-specific concerns:

**Index size.** A Chroma index for a 62-page PDF is a few megabytes and can ship inside the image. A large corpus needs a persistent volume or a hosted vector database, or your container becomes enormous and slow to deploy.

**Cold starts.** Free tiers sleep. A 40-second cold start during a live demo is painful. Either warm it before the demo, or add a "waking up..." state in the UI so the delay is explained rather than mysterious.

**Cost ceiling.** A public URL with your API key behind it is an open invitation. Add rate limiting and a hard budget cap:

```python
from fastapi import Request, HTTPException
from collections import defaultdict
import time

_hits = defaultdict(list)

def rate_limit(request: Request, max_per_hour: int = 30):
    ip = request.client.host
    now = time.time()
    _hits[ip] = [t for t in _hits[ip] if now - t < 3600]
    if len(_hits[ip]) >= max_per_hour:
        raise HTTPException(429, "Rate limit exceeded. Try again later.")
    _hits[ip].append(now)
```

Plus the `BudgetGuard` from Day 42. A demo that stops working because a bot exhausted your credits is worse than no demo.

##### Monitoring

Even for a portfolio project, wire in tracing and a feedback button. It costs an hour and it demonstrates production thinking.

```python
@app.post("/feedback")
async def feedback(req: FeedbackRequest):
    logger.info(json.dumps({
        "event": "feedback", "request_id": req.request_id,
        "rating": req.rating, "reason": req.reason, "ts": time.time(),
    }))
    return {"status": "recorded"}
```

In Gradio, add thumbs up/down to the chat interface. Then — and this is the part that matters — **actually review the negatives and report what you found**. "Of 340 sessions, 28 thumbs-down; 19 were Marathi retrieval failures, which is why v2 switched to multilingual-e5" is a sentence that demonstrates a working feedback loop.

##### The README

This is the highest-leverage hour in the entire capstone. Structure:

```markdown
# ScholarshipBot — [one line describing what it does for whom]

**[Live demo](url)** · **[3-min video](url)** · **[Architecture](#architecture)**

![demo gif](docs/demo.gif)

## The problem
[2-3 sentences. Who hurts, and how much.]

## What it does
[3-4 bullets, concrete and specific.]

## Results
| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Benchmark accuracy (20 Q) | 89% |
| Citation correctness | 95% |
| Refusal on out-of-scope | 5/5 |
| p95 latency | 4.2s |
| Cost per query | ₹0.09 |

[The progression table — this shows engineering.]

## Architecture
[Mermaid diagram]
[One line per component explaining why it is there.]

## Key technical decisions
- **multilingual-e5 over all-MiniLM** — Marathi retrieval went 0.41 → 0.79
- **Reranker** — +5pts page-hit for +1.2s latency; acceptable for this use case
- **Never give eligibility verdicts** — legal risk; we surface criteria only

## Limitations
[Honest. This section builds credibility.]

## Run it locally
make setup && make ingest && make serve

## Evaluation
make eval    # regenerates eval/results.csv

## Tech stack
[Table]
```

**Three things separate a good README from a bad one:**

1. **Lead with the problem and the live link**, not the tech stack.
2. **Numbers.** "89% on 20 benchmark questions" beats "works well."
3. **A limitations section.** Overclaiming fails technical interviews; honest limits read as senior.

Add a screenshot or GIF. Most readers will never clone your repo, and an image is the only thing guaranteed to be seen.

##### The demo video

Three minutes. Rehearse it. Timing:

- **0:00–0:20 — The problem.** "Maharashtra's scholarship guidelines are 62 pages of English. Students in tier-3 towns can't parse them."
- **0:20–1:20 — Live demo.** Three queries: one straightforward, one in Marathi, one out-of-scope showing the refusal. **Show the refusal.** It is more impressive than a correct answer, because it demonstrates you thought about failure.
- **1:20–2:20 — Architecture and one hard decision.** Screen-share the diagram; explain the multilingual embedding finding with the before/after numbers.
- **2:20–3:00 — Results and limitations.** The metrics table, then one honest weakness and how you would fix it.

Record with Loom or OBS. Do not over-produce it — clear audio and a steady screen recording are enough. Many reviewers will watch a three-minute video who would never clone a repo.

##### The polish checklist

- [ ] Live URL that works right now
- [ ] README leads with problem, demo link, and a screenshot
- [ ] Results table with real numbers
- [ ] Progression table showing what each change bought
- [ ] Architecture diagram in the repo
- [ ] Limitations section written honestly
- [ ] `make setup && make ingest && make serve` works from a clean clone
- [ ] Dependencies pinned; `.env.example` present; `.env` gitignored
- [ ] Guardrails active, with false-positive rate reported
- [ ] Rate limiting and a budget cap on the public endpoint
- [ ] Tracing and a feedback button
- [ ] At least a few tests
- [ ] Meaningful commit history
- [ ] 3-minute video linked
- [ ] Someone outside your course has used it successfully

That last item is the real test. Watch a stranger use it for five minutes and you will find three problems you were blind to.

##### Common mistakes

- **A README that starts with the tech stack** instead of the problem.
- **No live link**, so nobody sees it working.
- **No numbers** — "it works well" means nothing.
- **No limitations section**, which reads as inexperience or concealment.
- **A demo video over five minutes**, which nobody finishes.
- **Demoing only the happy path** and never the refusal.
- **No rate limiting on a public endpoint**, exhausting your API credits.
- **Reporting only aggregate metrics**, hiding a weak language or category.
- **Broken setup instructions** — always test from a fresh clone.
- **Leaving the eval set out of the repo**, making your numbers unverifiable.
- **Polishing the code and neglecting the presentation.** The presentation is what gets read.

##### Hands-on: finish it properly

Your practical task adds guardrails and an evaluation report, then deploys publicly with monitoring. Run the evaluation *before* and *after* adding guardrails so you can show they did not degrade legitimate answers — that pair of numbers is exactly what a reviewer wants and almost nobody provides.

The mini project is the finished, deployed capstone with a polished UI and comprehensive README. Budget a full day for the README, video, and screenshots. It will feel like it is not "real work" compared to code. It is the work that determines whether the code is ever seen.

The assignment is the 3-minute video and technical README. Record the video three times minimum — the first take is always too long and too vague. Then send the repo link to someone technical who has never seen it and ask two questions: "what does this do?" and "would you clone it?" Their answers tell you what to fix.

##### Key takeaways

- **The README is the deliverable most people actually consume** — lead with the problem, a live link, a screenshot, and real numbers.
- **Report metrics broken down by category and language**, not just an aggregate; the gap is where the useful finding lives.
- **The progression table is what demonstrates engineering** — showing what each change bought proves you measured rather than guessed.
- **Demo the refusal, not just the correct answer.** Showing that your system knows what it does not know is more impressive than another right answer.
- **A limitations section builds credibility**, and a public endpoint needs rate limiting and a budget cap before you share the URL.
